newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voters relatively unconcerned about scandals.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voters relatively unconcerned about scandals.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

A majority of American voters believe President Bill Clinton acted illegally or unethically in the Whitewater affair but most do not consider this or other alleged scandals to be very important, according to a Reuters public opinion poll released on Friday.

In the poll of 1,008 registered voters, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby International on Jan. 25-29, 24 percent of respondents said Clinton had acted illegally in the complex web of financial deals known collectively as Whitewater.

Nearly 35 percent thought he had acted unethically but not illegally, 18 percent said he had done nothing wrong and 23 percent were unsure. The poll carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton fared worse than her husband in the poll. Some 31 percent thought she had acted illegally and an additional 29 percent believed she had acted unethically, 16 percent said she had done nothing wrong and 24 percent were unsure.

Respondents were asked to rank the importance they attached to four scandals: Whitewater; foreign contributions to the Democratic National Committee; the sexual harrassment charges filed against Clinton by former Arkansas state employee Paula Jones and the ethical violations acknowleged by Republican House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich.

None of those issues were viewed as being very important by a majority of voters polled. The top concern, rated as very important by nearly 47 percent, was the foreign contributions to the Democratic Party, which are being investigated by the U.S. Justice Department and will soon be the subject of a congressional probe and hearings.
Just over 41 percent rated Gingrich's violations as very important and more than 58 percent of voters, including 49 percent of Republicans, felt he should step down as Speaker.
Gingrich, who this month was reprimanded by the House and told to pay a $300,000 penalty for ethical violations, had a 63 percent unfavourable rating in the poll.
Only 28 percent of respondents felt the Clintons' involvement in Whitewater was very important and some 27 percent thought Jones' sexual harassment allegations were very important.

Asked who they believed in the Paula Jones case, 29 percent said they believed Jones, 25 percent believed the president, who has denied wrongdoing, 19 percent believed neither and 27 percent were unsure.
But 55 percent felt Clinton should not face court action while he was still president. That issue is currently before the Supreme Court.

The various allegations against Clinton did not dent his generally positive ratings. When asked how they viewed the president, 65 percent of respondents said their overall impression of him was favourable, against 34 percent who viewed him unfavourably.

Not surprisingly, there was a wide partisan split in the way voters viewed Clinton with Republicans two to three times more likely than Democrats to believe the worst of him and his wife. Independent voters were somewhere between the extremes.
